lines: The plant operations lead says exactly one sentence: we want real-time dashboards for the plants.
One engineer hears that sentence and builds a genuinely streaming pipeline feeding a sub-second operator display.
A second engineer hears the very same sentence and builds a minutes-refresh aggregate dashboard instead. Both of them read those six words entirely faithfully.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
That plant lead genuinely isn't an engineer, and almost certainly has no technical definition of real-time sitting anywhere in their head.
Asking them to define that exact term more precisely isn't actually going to fork anything. So what question actually would?
answer: That lead doesn't actually have a technical definition sitting around to hand you.
What they genuinely do have is a behavior: some specific thing they actually go do the instant that number changes on screen.
That behavior is precisely the question that turns an otherwise vague demand into something concrete enough to actually check against.

lines: That plant lead's own box flips wide open to reveal three entirely different consumers already quietly reading this exact same data.
A quality report depends on it. A maintenance model depends on it too. So does a monthly compliance filing, sitting there the whole time.
Nobody in that first meeting ever actually asked about any of those three, yet the finished design still has to serve every single one.
A dashboard and a quality report can genuinely share one single warehouse aggregate between them without much trouble.
A maintenance model, on the other hand, needs its history held point-in-time correct, which is a fundamentally different requirement entirely.
A compliance filing needs something immutable and fully reproducible on demand. One single dataset, four genuinely different serving-store answers.
Real-time, said entirely on its own, isn't actually checkable against anything concrete.
I walk the floor the instant that number crosses a particular line is something else entirely: a real, stated trigger for real action.
That one sentence names the actual bound this freshness design now has to meet, rather than some borrowed adjective lifted straight out of a sales deck.
Four of these five answers are things the lead stated to you directly, right there in the room: how many lines, how often they actually check, how far back that filing has to reach.
The fifth answer, concerning where tenant count heads next year, is nothing more than an educated guess.
That one guess gets marked plainly as a guess, rather than quietly treated the exact same way as the other four, stated answers around it.
The level of detail each consumer genuinely needs gets asked up front, well before any model actually gets built around it.
How many people query all at once during that one Monday-morning report run matters just as much.
And how far back that filing genuinely has to be able to reprocess matters every bit as much as either of those.
A csv download and a bi extract both flip over to a stark red.
Each one of those two paths leaves the engine's own access policy behind completely, the instant that data actually crosses that particular boundary.
Which means an export path has to be designed around deliberately from the very start, never simply discovered later, well after the fact.
List every single consumer of the data, never only the one who happened to ask first.
Tie freshness directly to whatever that consumer actually does the moment they genuinely see the number.
Mark a bet plainly as a bet. Ask for grain, concurrency, and retention well up front. And treat every export path as its own policy gap, one that genuinely needs designing around.
One more, to use this for real: an entirely new prompt arrives, asking for a single view of the customer.
That prompt names a noun, nothing more — not a consumer, not a freshness bound, not a grain.
Does this design simply start from that noun directly, or does it start from those same five questions all over again?
answer: A single view of the customer is exactly as vague as real-time dashboards for the plants ever was.
It's a noun quietly standing in for a design nobody has actually specified yet, in any real detail.
Those same five questions fork this entirely new prompt in exactly the same way they forked the very first one.
